$$ \displaystyle\frac{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}{p_{k_{l}}}\cdot(1-p_{+})=\frac{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}{p_{k_{l}}}\cdot\sum_{k\in I}p_{k}(1-q_{k})=\sum_{k\in I}p_{m_{1}-k}=1-p_{-}=1-o(1). $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle Z^{(2c)} \displaystyle\asymp\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\asymp n^{3/2}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(2c)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\asymp 1. $$

By Bernstein’s inequality, for any $\delta_{1}>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|E^{(2a)}_{-}\right|\geq\delta_{1}n^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

So for small enough $\delta_{1}>0$ , with probability $1-o(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle~\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle~\frac{1}{Z^{(2c)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\left(\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}-\sum_{e\in E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\right) \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\left(n^{3/2}-\delta_{1}n^{2}\cdot n^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~1, $$

where in the second-to-last step we used Corollary 5.23, Items (i) and (iii), and $\left|E^{(2a)}_{-}\right|\leq\delta_{1}n^{2}$ .

Summarizing the above, at the end of Step 2c, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0})=\Theta(1), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})=\Theta(1). $$

### 5.6 Phase 3

In Phase 3, the algorithm makes $c_{2}n^{2}$ adaptive exact queries. We show that for $c_{2}>0$ small enough, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , the algorithm will not be able to return the correct answer.

Let $E^{(3)}$ be the set of edges queried in Phase 3. We can w.l.o.g. assume that $E^{(3)}\subseteq E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}$ , because only queries in this set are useful. Conditioned on $G$ being connected, the probability that $E^{(3)}$ hits the edge $e^{*}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{e\in E^{(3)}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})}{\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})}\leq c_{2}n^{2}\cdot\Theta(n^{-2})\asymp c_{2}, $$

which is $1-\Omega(1)$ for $c_{2}>0$ small enough. Therefore, for small enough $c_{2}$ , with probability $\Omega(1)$ , $E^{(3)}$ does not hit the edge $e^{*}$ .

Conditioned on $E^{(3)}$ does not hit $e^{*}$ , let $\mathbb{P}^{(3)}$ denote the posterior distribution of the original graph $G$ given all observations. We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(G_{0}), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash\left(E^{(2a)}_{-}\cup E^{(3)}\right)}\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(G_{e}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(3)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(3)}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}, \displaystyle Z^{(3)} \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}+\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash\left(E^{(2a)}_{-}\cup E^{(3)}\right)}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}. $$

By the same discussion as in the end of Phase 2, Step 2c, for $c_{2}>0$ small enough, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\Theta(1), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\Theta(1). $$

In this case, any return value would lead to an error probability of $\Omega(1)$ .

This concludes the proof of Proposition 5.18.

### 5.7 $s$ - $t$ Connectivity

In this section we modify the proof of Theorem 1.2 to show hardness of $s$ - $t$ Connectivity. Recall the $s$ - $t$ Connectivity problem, where the input is an unknown undirected graph on $n$ labeled vertices, and a pair of vertices $s,t\in V$ . An algorithm can make noisy queries to edge membership and the goal is to determine whether $s$ and $t$ are in the same connected component of $G$ .

#### Proposition 5.24 (Hardness of $s$ - $t$ Connectivity).

Any algorithm that solves the $s$ - $t$ Connectivity problem with $\frac{1}{3}$ error probability uses $\Omega(n^{2}\log n)$ noisy queries in expectation.

#### Proof.

As discussed in Section 2.2, the error probability in the proposition statement can be replaced with any $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}$ , and the expected number of queries can be replaced with worst-case number of queries.

We design an input distribution for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity by generating $G$ from Definition 5.15, and choosing $s,t$ i.i.d. $\sim\Unif(V)$ .

Then we run the same proof as Theorem 1.2. That is, we define a three-phase problem for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity, where the oracle uses the same strategy in Phase 2 as in Graph Connectivity. Because $s$ and $t$ are independent with $G$ , in the end of Phase 2, conditioned on Step 2c does not report failure, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , $s\in T_{1}$ and $t\in T_{2}$ . In this case, $s$ - $t$ Connectivity is equivalent to Graph Connectivity. In the proof of Graph Connectivity, we have shown that with probability $\Omega(1)$ (over the randomness of the graph and Phase 1 and 2), any algorithm that uses at most $c_{2}n^{2}$ queries in Phase 3 has $\Omega(1)$ error probability. This implies that the same holds for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity. ∎

## 6 Threshold and Counting

In this section we present our proof for Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 1.4. We use $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ to denote $k$ -Threshold problem with input length $n$ .

### 6.1 Lower bound for $k$ -Threshold

In this section we prove the lower bound part of Theorem 1.3. That is, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ for $k\leq 2n-1$ requires at least $(1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation. The $k=o(n)$ case has been proved in [WGZW24] (see also Appendix A for our alternative and simpler proof).

#### Theorem 6.1.

For $k=o(n)$ , solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, even when the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k-1}$ with probability $1/2$ .

In our lower bound proof, we will use Theorem 6.1 with $k=O(n/\log n)$ .

We first prove the case where $k=(n+1)/2$ .

#### Lemma 6.2.

Solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, even when the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ with probability $1/2$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that we have an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that solves $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ and uses only $(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $\epsilon>0$ . Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution of inputs where with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ , and with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ . Now we consider two cases, depending on whether the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ make on indices with $1$ ’s is larger or not. In either case, we will use $\mathcal{A}$ to obtain an algorithm more efficient than the lower bound in Theorem 6.1, thus reaching a contradiction.

First, suppose $\mathcal{A}$ makes more queries in expectation on indices with $1$ ’s under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . Let $k^{\prime}=\Theta(k/\log k)$ and let $n=k-1+k^{\prime}$ . Consider an instance of $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n}$ where the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k^{\prime}}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k^{\prime}-1}$ with probability $1/2$ . By Theorem 6.1, this instance requires $(1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{\prime}}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ queries in expectation. We will design an algorithm $\mathcal{B}$ solving such an instance utilizing $\mathcal{A}$ .

When $\mathcal{B}$ gets the input, it first adds $2k-1-n$ $1$ ’s to the input, and then randomly shuffle the indices. Then $\mathcal{B}$ sends this input to $\mathcal{A}$ . Whenever $\mathcal{A}$ makes a query to a $1$ that is artificially added, $\mathcal{B}$ simulates a noisy query using random bits; when $\mathcal{A}$ makes a query to an actual input, $\mathcal{B}$ makes a query as well and pass the result to $\mathcal{A}$ . When $\mathcal{A}$ returns a result, $\mathcal{B}$ returns the same result. It is not difficult to verify that the input distribution for $\mathcal{A}$ is exactly $\mathcal{D}$ . Also, whenever the input to $\mathcal{A}$ has at least $k$ $1$ ’s, the input to $\mathcal{B}$ has $k^{\prime}$ $1$ ’s, and vice versa, so the correct output of $\mathcal{A}$ is the same as the correct output of $\mathcal{B}$ . Therefore, $\mathcal{B}$ is correct whenever $\mathcal{A}$ is correct, which happens with probability $\delta$ .

Next, we analyze the expected number of queries $\mathcal{B}$ makes, which consist of two parts:

- • The number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes to an actual $0$ in the input: Because we are in the case where $\mathcal{A}$ makes more queries in expectation on indices with $1$ ’s in the input than indices with $0$ ’s, the expected number of this type of queries is at most half of the expected total number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes. Thus, the number of queries in this case is at most $(1-\epsilon)\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ .

- • The number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes to an actual $1$ in the input: Each actual $1$ in the input to $\mathcal{B}$ is later permuted to a random position in the sequence. By symmetry, a random $1$ in the input to $\mathcal{A}$ under the input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is queried at most $\frac{1}{k-1}\cdot(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ times in expectation. The number of actual $1$ ’s is $k^{\prime}=\Theta(k/\log k)$ , so the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on them is $\frac{k^{\prime}}{k-1}\cdot(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=o(1)\cdot\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ .

As a result, the total number of queries $\mathcal{B}$ makes is $(1-\epsilon)\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ , which contradicts Theorem 6.1.

For the second case where $\mathcal{A}$ makes more (or equal number of) queries in expectation on indices with $0$ ’s under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . The only difference is that, when $\mathcal{B}$ sends the input to $\mathcal{A}$ , it has to flip the roles of $0$ ’s and $1$ ’s. Additionally, it has to flip the result $\mathcal{A}$ returns. We omit the details. ∎

Given Theorem 6.1 and Lemma 6.2, we are ready to prove the lower bound for general $k$ .

#### Theorem 6.3.

Solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation for $n/\log n\leq k\leq n/2$ .

#### Proof.

The high-level proof strategy is similar to that of Lemma 6.2, by reducing from a hard instance to $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ . However, the difference is that we need to reduce from two different cases depending on whether the average number of queries per $1$ or per $0$ is larger. In Lemma 6.2 we did not have to do it because we can simply flip all the $0$ ’s and $1$ ’s in the input and retain the same problem as $n=2k-1$ .

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[n]}{k}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[n]}{k-1}$ . Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ using $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $\epsilon>0$ . Let $q_{0}$ denote the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on a random index with input value $0$ (under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ ), and let $q_{1}$ denote the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on a random index with input value $1$ (under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ ). Let $Q$ be the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes.

Consider the following two cases: $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ and $q_{0}>q_{1}$ .

#### Case $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ .

Let $k^{\prime}=\Theta(n/\log n)\leq k$ and let $n^{\prime}=n-k+k^{\prime}$ . Note that $n^{\prime}\in[n/2,n]$ , so we have $k^{\prime}=\Theta(n^{\prime}/\log n^{\prime})$ . By Theorem 6.1, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n^{\prime}}$ under input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[n^{\prime}]}{k^{\prime}}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[n^{\prime}]}{k^{\prime}-1}$ with error probability $\delta$ requires $(1-o(1))\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{k^{\prime}}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation.

Given an instance of $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n^{\prime}}$ , we add $n-n^{\prime}$ artificial $1$ ’s to the input, and then randomly permute the input, and feed it to $\mathcal{A}$ . If $\mathcal{A}$ queries an actual input, we also make an actual query; if $\mathcal{A}$ queries an artificial input, we can simulate a query without making an actual query. Finally, we use the result returned by $\mathcal{A}$ as our answer. It is not difficult to verify that this algorithm is correct with error probability $\delta$ , and the input distribution to $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathcal{D}$ .

Let us analyze the expected number of queries $Q^{\prime}$ used by the algorithm, which can be expressed as follows:

$$ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}(k^{\prime}-1)+q_{0}(n-k+1)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}k^{\prime}+q_{0}(n-k)\right). $$

Also, notice that the number of queries $Q$ made by $\mathcal{A}$ under input $\mathcal{D}$ is

$$ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}(k-1)+q_{0}(n-k+1)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}k+q_{0}(n-k)\right). $$

As $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ , the above implies that $q_{1}\geq Q/n$ . Furthermore, we have that $Q-Q^{\prime}=q_{1}\cdot(k-k^{\prime})=q_{1}\cdot(n-n^{\prime})\geq\frac{n-n^{\prime}}{n}\cdot Q$ . Therefore,

$$ Q^{\prime}\leq\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\cdot Q\leq(1-\epsilon)\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\leq(1-\epsilon)\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}, $$

which contradicts Theorem 6.1.

#### Case $q_{0}>q_{1}$ .

By Lemma 6.2, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ under input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ with error probability $\delta$ requires $(1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation.

Given such an input to $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ , we add $n-2k+1$ artificial $0$ ’s to the input, and then randomly permute the input, and feed it to $\mathcal{A}$ . Similar as before, we make an actual query if $\mathcal{A}$ queries an actual input, and we simulate a query otherwise. It is not difficult to verify that this algorithm is correct with error probability $\delta$ , and the input distribution to $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathcal{D}$ .

The expected number of actual queries used by the algorithm can be similarly analyzed as the previous case, which can be upper bounded by $(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)},$ contradicting Lemma 6.2. ∎

### 6.2 Upper bound for $k$ -Threshold

In this section we prove our upper bound for $k$ -Threshold, stated as follows.

#### Theorem 6.4.

Given a sequence $a\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ and an integer $1\leq k\leq n$ , there is an algorithm that can output $\min\{k,\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ using

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### 6.2.1 Preliminaries

The following lemmas are standard.

#### Lemma 6.5 (e.g., [GX23, WGZW24]).

For a bit $B$ , there is an algorithm $\textup{{Check-Bit}}(B,\delta)$ that can return the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### Lemma 6.6 (e.g., [Fel70]).

Consider a biased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$ . At each time step, the walk adds $1$ to the current value with probability $p<1/2$ , and adds $-1$ to the current value with probability $1-p$ . Then the probability that the random walk ever reaches some integer $x\geq 0$ is $(p/(1-p))^{x}$ .

#### Lemma 6.7 (e.g., [Fel70]).

Consider a biased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$ . At each time step, the walk adds $1$ to the current value with probability $p<1/2$ , and adds $-1$ to the current value with probability $1-p$ . Then the expected number of steps needed to first reach some integer $-x\leq 0$ is $\frac{x}{1-2p}$ .

Our algorithm for $k$ -Threshold and Counting uses the following asymmetric version of Check-Bit.

#### Lemma 6.8.

For a bit $B$ , there is an algorithm $\textup{{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}}(B,\delta_{0},\delta_{1})$ such that:

- • If the actual value of $B$ is $0$ , then the algorithm returns the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta_{0}$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta_{1}}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta_{1}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

- • If the actual value of $B$ is $1$ , then the algorithm returns the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta_{1}$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta_{0}}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta_{0}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### Proof.

Let $a$ and $b$ be two integer parameters to be set later. The algorithm works as follows: we keep querying the input bit, and keep track of the number of queries that returns $1$ (denoted by $q_{1}$ ) and the number of queries that returns $0$ (denoted by $q_{0}$ ). We stop once $q_{1}-q_{0}=-a$ , in which case we declare the bit to be $0$ , or $q_{1}-q_{0}=b$ , in which case we declare the bit to be $1$ .

If the input bit is $1$ , then the probability that the algorithm returns $0$ can be upper bounded by $\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{a}$ using Lemma 6.6, so by setting $a=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta_{1})}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , this probability is upper bounded by $\delta_{1}$ .

On the other hand, if the input bit is $0$ , then the probability that the algorithm returns $1$ can be upper bounded by $\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{b}$ using Lemma 6.6, so by setting $b=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta_{0})}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , this probability is upper bounded by $\delta_{0}$ .

Now we consider the expected running time of the algorithm. First suppose the input bit is $1$ , then the algorithm can be viewed as a random walk on integers starting at $0$ , and each time it adds $1$ with probability $1-p$ and subtracts $1$ with probability $p$ . It stops once the random walk reaches $-a$ or $b$ . This stopping time is upper bounded by the first time it reaches $b$ , and the expected number of steps required for it to first reach $b$ is $\frac{b}{1-2p}=(1+o_{1/\delta_{0}}(1))\frac{\log(1/\delta_{0})}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ by Lemma 6.7. Similarly, if the input bit is $0$ , then the expected number of queries used by the algorithm is upper bounded by $(1+o_{1/\delta_{1}}(1))\frac{\log(1/\delta_{1})}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ . ∎

#### 6.2.2 The proof

We are now ready to state our proof of Theorem 6.4.

Our algorithm is extremely simple and is outlined in Algorithm 1. It repeatedly calls the subroutine $\textsc{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}(a_{i},\delta/2n,\delta/2k)$ from Lemma 6.8 for every $i\in[n]$ , and uses the returned value as the guess for $a_{i}$ . If at any point, the current number of $a_{i}$ whose guess is $1$ reaches $k$ , the algorithm terminates early and return $k$ . Otherwise, the algorithm returns the number of $a_{i}$ whose guess is $1$ at the end.

*Algorithm 1*

```
1: procedure Threshold-Count( $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\},k,\delta$ )
2: $cnt=0$
3: for $i=1\to n$ do
4: $cnt=cnt+\textsc{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}(a_{i},\delta/2n,\delta/2k)$
5: if $cnt\geq k$ then return $k$
6: return $cnt$
```

#### Error probability.

We first analyze the error probability of the algorithm. First, suppose $\lVert a\rVert_{1}\geq k$ . Let $S\subseteq[n]$ be an arbitrary size- $k$ set where $a_{i}=1$ for $i\in S$ . Then by the guarantee of Asymmetric-Check-Bit, for every $i\in S$ , the probability that the guess for $a_{i}$ is not $1$ is $\leq\delta/2k$ . Therefore, by union bound, the guesses for $a_{i}$ for all $i\in S$ are $1$ with probability $\geq 1-\delta/2$ . Therefore, the count will be at least $k$ so the algorithm will return $k$ as the correct answer with error probability $\leq\delta/2\leq\delta$ .

If $\lVert a\rVert_{1}<k$ , then by union bound, the probability that all guesses are correct is $\geq 1-\frac{\delta}{2k}\cdot\lVert a\rVert_{1}-\frac{\delta}{2n}\cdot(1-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\geq 1-\delta$ , so the returned count of the algorithm is also correct with probability $\geq 1-\delta$ .

#### Expected number of queries.

We first consider the number of $a_{i}$ with $a_{i}=1$ that we pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit. One trivial upper bound is $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ . Also, the expected number of $a_{i}=1$ we need to pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit before $cnt$ is incremented by $1$ is $\leq\frac{1}{1-\delta/2k}$ , so another upper bound is $\frac{k}{1-\delta/2k}\leq(1+o(1))k$ (as $\delta=o(1)$ ). On the other hand, the number of $a_{i}$ where $a_{i}=0$ that we pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit is upper bounded by $n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ . Note that whether we pass some $a_{i}$ to Asymmetric-Check-Bit only depends on the queries we make to $a_{i^{\prime}}$ for $i^{\prime}<i$ , so even given that we pass some $a_{i}$ to Asymmetric-Check-Bit, we can still use the bounds from Lemma 6.8 to bound the expected number of queries we make to $a_{i}$ . Therefore, the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ (1+o(1))\left(\min\left\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},k\right\}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right). $$

Then we consider two cases depending on how large $k$ is.

#### Case $k\geq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $\log(n)=(1+o(1))\log k$ , so the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(\min\left\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},k\right\}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

#### Case $k\leq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $k\log\frac{n}{\delta}=o(n\log\frac{k}{\delta})$ , so the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+n\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

### 6.3 Bounds for Counting

Let us first prove a one-sided upper bound for Counting.

#### Theorem 6.9.

Given a sequence $a\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ , there is an algorithm that can output $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ using

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

The difference between Theorem 6.9 and the upper bound part of Theorem 1.4 is that we have $\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1$ rather than $\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1,n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1\}$ inside the log term.

#### Proof.

Outlined in Algorithm 2, the algorithm for counting is an adaptation of Algorithm 1. Notice that in Algorithm 1, when calling Asymmetric-Check-Bit, we have $\delta_{0}=\delta/2n$ and $\delta_{1}=\delta/2k$ . The value $\delta_{0}$ is fixed regardless of the value of $k$ , and the value $\delta_{1}$ depends on $k$ . The algorithm for counting in some sense is simulating Algorithm 1, but dynamically adjusting $\delta_{1}$ based on the current estimate of $k$ , which is the number of input bits that are believed to be $1$ ’s.

For simplicity, throughout the analysis, we use $k^{*}=\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ to denote the desired answer. Let $S_{0}\subseteq[n]$ be indices $i$ with $a_{i}=0$ and let $S_{1}=[n]\backslash S_{0}$ .

*Algorithm 2*

```
1: procedure Counting( $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\},\delta$ )
2: $k\leftarrow 0$
3: $c\leftarrow\{0\}^{n}$
4: $Active\leftarrow[n]$
5: while True do
6: $i^{*}\leftarrow\argmax_{i\in Active}c_{i}$
7: if $c_{i^{*}}\leq-\frac{\log(6(k+1)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}$ then return $k$
8: if $\textsc{Query}(a_{i^{*}})=1$ then
9: $c_{i^{*}}=c_{i^{*}}+1$
10: if $c_{i^{*}}\geq\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}$ then
11: $Active\leftarrow Active\backslash\{i^{*}\}$
12: $k\leftarrow k+1$
13: else
14: $c_{i^{*}}=c_{i^{*}}-1$
```

#### Error probability.

For any $i$ , we can view the value of $c_{i}$ as a random walk, i.e., after every query to $a_{i}$ , we either adds $1$ to $c_{i}$ or subtracts $1$ from $c_{i}$ . If $c_{i}=1$ , then the probability that we add $1$ to $c_{i}$ after every step is $1-p$ , and the probability that we subtract $1$ is $p$ . If $c_{i}=0$ , then the probability that we add $1$ to $c_{i}$ after every step is $p$ , and the probability that we subtract $1$ is $1-p$ . Conceptually, we can view $c_{i}$ as an infinite random walk, and the algorithm only utilizes some prefix of it.

For $i\in S_{1}$ , by Lemma 6.6, the probability that $c_{i}$ ever reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is at most

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\delta/6. $$

Furthermore, if some $c_{i}$ never reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , then $i$ will eventually be removed from $Active$ and contributes towards $k$ . Since the random walks $c_{i}$ ’s are independent for different $i$ ’s, the probability that there are $\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1$ many $i\in S_{1}$ where $c_{i}$ reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ can be upper bounded by

$$ \binom{k^{*}}{\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1}\cdot(\delta/6)^{\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1}\leq 2^{k^{*}}(\delta/6)^{k^{*}/2+1}\leq(1.5\delta)^{k^{*}/2}\cdot(\delta/6)\leq\delta/6, $$

where the last step holds because $\delta=o(1)$ and hence we can assume $1.5\delta\leq 1$ . Thus, up to $\delta/6$ error probability, the number of $i\in S_{1}$ that contributes towards $k$ is at least $k^{*}-(\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1)$ , which means the final value of $k$ is $\geq\max\{0,k^{*}-(\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1)\}=\max\{0,\lfloor k^{*}/2\rfloor-1\}$ . This further implies that $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ . Let $E_{1}$ be the event $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ and as analyzed above, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1})\leq\delta/6$ .

Next, we consider the event $E_{2}$ where all $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{1}$ never reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.6, the probability that each $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{1}$ reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is upper bounded by

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\frac{\delta}{2k^{*}}. $$

Therefore, by union bound, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{2})\leq\delta/2$ .

Next, let $E_{3}$ be the event where all $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ never reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.6, the probability that each $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is upper bounded by

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\frac{\delta}{6n}. $$

Therefore, by union bound, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{3})\leq\delta/6$ .

Assume $E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}$ all happen. Then we know that $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ , and so all $i\in S_{1}$ will eventually be removed from $Active$ and contribute towards $k$ . Also, all $i\in S_{0}$ will not contribute towards $k$ . Therefore, the returned value of $k$ will be equal to $k^{*}$ . Hence, the error probability of the algorithm is upper bounded by $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1}\vee\neg E_{2}\vee\neg E_{3})\leq\delta/6+\delta/2+\delta/6\leq\delta$ .

#### Expected number of queries.

Next, we analyze the expected number of queries used by the algorithm.

First, for every $i\in S_{1}$ , the expected number of times we query $a_{i}$ is upper bounded by the expected number of steps it takes for the random walk $c_{i}$ takes to reach $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.7, it is bounded by

$$ \frac{\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil}{1-2p}=(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Then we consider the expected number of times we query $a_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ . Fix any $i\in S_{0}$ . Let $F_{j}$ be the event where for exactly $j$ distinct $i^{\prime}\in S_{0}\backslash\{i\}$ , the infinite random walk $c_{j}$ ever reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By analysis in the error probability part, $\mathbb{P}(F_{j})\leq\binom{n}{j}\cdot(\delta/6n)^{j}\leq\delta^{j}$ . Note that $F_{j}$ is independent with the random walk $c_{i}$ . If $F_{j}$ holds, then the number of times we query $a_{i}$ is upper bounded by the expected number of steps it takes for the random walk $c_{i}$ first hits $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}+j+1))/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ (because once $c_{i}$ hits this value, $k$ can never be larger than $k^{*}+j$ under $F_{j}$ , so we will not query $a_{i}$ again). By Lemma 6.7, this expectation is

$$ \frac{\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}+j+1))/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil}{1-2p}=(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+j+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Let $Q_{i}$ be the number of times we query $a_{i}$ . Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Q_{i}) \displaystyle=\sum_{j\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(Q_{i}|F_{j})\cdot\mathbb{P}(F_{j}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+j+1}{\delta}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{(k^{*}+1)(j+1)}{\delta}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}\right)+\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log(j+1)\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}\right)+O(1)\right) \displaystyle\leq(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Summing up everything, the overall expected number of queries is

$$ (1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-k^{*})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right). $$

Similar to the proof of Theorem 6.4, we consider two cases depending on how large $k^{*}$ is.

#### Case $k^{*}\geq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $\log(n)=(1+o(1))\log(k^{*}+1)$ , so the expected number of queries can be bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-k^{*})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

#### Case $k^{*}\leq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $k^{*}\log\frac{n}{\delta}=o(n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta})$ , so the expected number of queries can be bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+n\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

∎

#### Proof.

$$ (1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $c>0$ . First, suppose $\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2$ . $$ (1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{k+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}, $$

which contradicts the lower bound for $k$ -Threshold.

If $\lVert a\rVert_{1}>n/2$ , we can simply first flip all the bits in the $k$ -Threshold instance, and then use the same argument.

For the upper bound, given Theorem 6.9, it suffices to first estimate whether $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ is bigger than $n/2$ or smaller. When it is smaller, we can directly run Theorem 6.9; otherwise, we first flip all input bits and then run Theorem 6.9.

More precisely, we randomly sample $n^{0.99}$ input elements with replacements, use Lemma 6.5 to estimate them with error probability $1/n^{100}$ . If the fraction of elements in the sample whose estimates are $1$ is $\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , we directly call Theorem 6.9 with error bound $\delta$ and return the result; otherwise, we flip all input bits, call Theorem 6.9 with error bound $\delta$ , and return $n$ minus the result.

Regardless of whether we flip the input bits, the output is always correct assuming the returned result of Theorem 6.9 is correct. Therefore, the error probability of the algorithm is at most $\delta$ .

Next, we analyze the expected running time of the algorithm. Let $E_{1}$ be the event that the fraction of sampled elements that are $1$ is within $n^{-0.01}$ of the fraction of all elements that are $1$ . By Chernoff bound,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1})\leq 2e^{-2\left(n^{-0.01}\right)^{2}\cdot n^{0.99}}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{n^{99}}\right). $$

$$ \mathbb{P}(\neg E_{2})\leq\frac{1}{n^{99}}. $$

If $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ both hold, the expected number of queries of Theorem 6.9 can be bounded as

$$ (1+o(1))\cdot\frac{n}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\cdot\begin{cases}\log\frac{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1}{\delta},&\text{if }\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2-n^{0.99},\\
\log\frac{n+1}{\delta},&\text{if }n/2-n^{0.99}<\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2+n^{0.99},\\

$$ (1+o(1))\cdot\frac{n\log\frac{n+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Therefore, the overall expected number of queries can be bounded as

$$ \displaystyle n^{0.99}\cdot(1+o(1))\cdot\frac{\log\frac{1}{n^{100}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1}\vee\neg E_{2})(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{n+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

as desired. ∎

for $B\in\mathcal{C}^{(2b)}$ . In particular, $\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)},A_{-}^{(2a)},|A|\right)$ is a sufficient statistic for $A$ at the end of Step 2b.

We note that $\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|<k$ with probability $\geq\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}$ because

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\Bin(k,1-p_{+})>0\right)=1-p_{+}^{k}\geq 1-\exp\left(k(1-p_{+})\right)\geq\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}. $$

#### Step 2c.

Let $A_{+}^{(2c)}$ be the set of elements in $I$ revealed in Step 2c but not in previous steps, and $A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}=A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\cup A_{+}^{(2c)}$ . Let $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ be the posterior distribution of $A$ and $\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}$ be the support of $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{(2c)} \displaystyle=\left\{A:A\in\binom{[n]}{k-1}\cup\binom{[n]}{k},A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\subseteq A\subseteq[n]\backslash A_{-}^{(2a)}\right\} \displaystyle=\left\{A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\right\}\cup\left\{A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup\{i\}:i\in[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\right)\right\}. $$

For simplicity of notation, define $A_{0}=A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}$ and $A_{i}=A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup\{i\}$ for $i\in[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\right)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(A_{0}) \displaystyle\propto\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(A_{0}), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(A_{i}) \displaystyle\propto\frac{1}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\cdot\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(A_{i}). $$

Recall that $\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(B)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\binom{n}{|B|}}$ for $|B|\in\{k-1,k\}$ . Let $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}$ (resp. $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}$ ) denote the probability measure of observations at the end of Step 2c conditioned on $|A|=k$ (resp. $|A|=k-1$ ). Summing over $i$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}=\left|[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\right)\right|\cdot\frac{1}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\cdot\frac{\binom{n}{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k}}. $$

#### Lemma A.4.

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}\left(\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}\leq\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2}\right)\geq\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}. $$

#### Proof.

Because $p_{-}=o(1)$ , with probability $1-o(1)$ , we have $\left|A_{-}^{(2a)}\right|\leq np_{-}^{1/2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\left|[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\right)\right|=n-(k-1)-A_{-}^{(2a)}=(1\pm o(1))n $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}} \displaystyle=(1\pm o(1))n\cdot\frac{1}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\cdot\frac{k}{n} \displaystyle=(1\pm o(1))\frac{k}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}. $$

Note that $k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|\sim\Bin(k,1-p_{+})$ , and $\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|$ is independent with $\left|A_{-}^{(2a)}\right|$ conditioned on $|A|$ . Recall that

$$ \displaystyle 1-p_{+}=(1\pm o(1))\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}=(\delta/k)^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}. $$

If $k^{\epsilon_{1}}\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}}\geq\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2}$ , then $k(1-p_{+})=\omega(1)$ and by concentration

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\Bin(k,1-p_{+})\geq\frac{1}{2}k(1-p_{+})\right)=1-o(1) $$

Under $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}$ , conditioned on $k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|\geq\frac{1}{2}k(1-p_{+})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}=(1\pm o(1))\frac{k}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}=O(1). $$

If $k^{\epsilon_{1}}\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}}\leq\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2}$ , then conditioned on $\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|<k$ (which happens with probability at least $\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}$ by Eq. 27), we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}=(1\pm o(1))\frac{k}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\leq\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2\pm o(1)}. $$

Combining both cases we finish the proof. ∎

From Lemma A.4 we can conclude that no algorithm can determine $|A|$ with error probability $\leq\delta$ at the end of Phase 2. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that such an algorithm exists. Let $\mathcal{E}$ denote the event that $\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}\leq\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2}$ . Under $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}$ , conditioned on $\mathcal{E}$ , the algorithm outputs “ $|A|=k$ ” with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$ (otherwise the overall error probability under $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}$ is at least $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\delta^{1-\epsilon\pm o(1)}$ ). However, this implies that under $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}$ , the algorithm outputs $|A|=k$ with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}\delta^{\epsilon_{1}/2}$ by definition of $\mathcal{E}$ .

### A.4 Phase 3

In Phase 3, the algorithm makes at most $(1-\epsilon_{2})n$ adaptive exact queries. If $\left|[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\right)\right|=(1\pm o(1))n$ , then with probability $(1\pm o(1))\epsilon_{2}$ , these exact queries do not hit any elements in $A$ . Let $\mathbb{P}^{(3)}_{k}$ (resp. $\mathbb{P}^{(3)}_{k-1}$ ) denote the probability measure of observations at the end of Phase 3 conditioned on $|A|=k$ (resp. $|A|=k-1$ ). Conditioned on that the exact queries do not hit any elements in $A$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}_{k-1}}=\left|[n]\backslash\left(A_{+}^{(\leq 2c)}\cup A_{-}^{(2a)}\cup A^{(3)}\right)\right|\cdot\frac{1}{k-\left|A_{+}^{(\leq 2b)}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\cdot\frac{\binom{n}{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k}} $$

where $A^{(3)}$ denotes the set of elements queried in Phase 3. By a similar proof as Lemma A.4, we can prove that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}_{k}\left(\frac{d\mathbb{P}^{(3)}_{k}}{d\mathbb{P}^{(3)}_{k-1}}\leq\epsilon_{2}^{-1}\delta^{-\epsilon_{1}/2}\right)\geq\epsilon_{2}\delta^{1-\epsilon_{1}\pm o(1)}. $$

However, $\epsilon_{2}$ is a constant, so the discussion in the end of Section A.3 still applies. This concludes that no algorithm can solve the three-phase problem with error probability $\leq\delta$ using at most $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries.
